title: Enzyme Engine
desc: CHEM 3B enzyme practice: classify enzymes from their reactions, identify inhibitors from active-site pictures, read activity-vs-temperature, pH and substrate graphs, match vitamins to coenzymes, and work regulation and clinical questions, plus final-exam practice.

subtitle: Classify enzymes, spot the inhibitor, read the activity graphs, and match every vitamin to its coenzyme.
tip: Most inhibitor questions come down to two things: does the inhibitor look like the substrate (competitive) and can it be removed (reversible)?
reference:
🧠 Reference: enzyme classes, inhibitors, vitamins
ClassWhat it doesExamples
Oxidoreductasemoves H or electrons (NAD+, FAD)dehydrogenases, oxidases, catalase
Transferasemoves a group between moleculeskinases, aminotransferases, citrate synthase
Hydrolasebreaks a bond with waterlipase, amylase, proteases, phosphatases
Lyaseadds/removes across a double bond, no water or ATPfumarase, aldolase, decarboxylases, carbonic anhydrase
Isomeraserearranges one moleculeisomerases, mutases, racemases
Ligasejoins two molecules using ATPDNA ligase, carboxylases, synthetases

Inhibitors: competitive (looks like substrate, active site, overcome by more substrate) · noncompetitive (other site, changes shape, not overcome) · irreversible (covalent: aspirin, penicillin, nerve agents) · heavy metals (bind –SH; irreversible and noncompetitive) · feedback (end product, allosteric). Activity rises with temperature until denaturation (~40 °C for human enzymes), peaks at an optimum pH (pepsin 2, trypsin 8, most others ~7), and plateaus when substrate saturates the active sites.

B vitamins → coenzymes: B1 TPP · B2 FAD · B3 NAD+ · B5 CoA · B6 PLP · B7 biotin · B9 THF · B12 cobalamin. Vitamin C: collagen (scurvy). Vitamin K: clotting. Fat-soluble A, D, E, K are stored; water-soluble B and C are not.
